title: AutoMem: Automated Learning of Memory as a Cognitive Skill
hook: AutoMem treats knowing what to remember and when to retrieve it — metamemory — as a trainable skill, and tuning memory alone roughly doubles to quadruples performance on long-horizon games.
key_points: Frames memory management as 'metamemory' — a learnable skill about what to encode, when to retrieve, and how to organize knowledge — and promotes filesystem operations to first-class memory actions alongside task actions.
Optimizes two axes automatically: the memory structure (prompts, file schemas, action vocabulary) and the model's proficiency at using it.

A strong LLM reviews complete agent trajectories to iteratively revise the memory structure; separately, the agent's own good memory decisions become training signal that sharpens memory proficiency directly.

Across Crafter, MiniHack, and NetHack, optimizing memory alone (task-action behavior untouched) improved a base agent ~2x-4x, making a 32B open model competitive with frontier systems like Claude Opus 4.5.
Shows memory management is an independently learnable skill, not just a byproduct of general capability.
content_html: Knowing what to remember, when to retrieve it, and how to organize it — metamemory, in cognitive-science terms — is treated by AutoMem as a skill an LLM agent can learn, not a fixed mechanism bolted on from outside. The authors promote filesystem operations to first-class memory actions alongside an agent's normal task actions, and let the model decide how to manage its own memory.
extra_html:
Two loops, two axes

Memory improves along two axes that both resist manual tuning: the structure supporting it (prompts, file schemas, the action vocabulary) and the model's proficiency at exercising it. AutoMem automates both. In the first loop, a strong LLM reviews complete agent trajectories — which can run for thousands of steps, long enough that a single memory mistake can hide before it surfaces — and iteratively revises the memory structure. In the second loop, the agent's own good memory decisions, identified across many episodes, become training signal that directly sharpens the model's memory proficiency.

Why it matters

Across three procedurally generated long-horizon games — Crafter, MiniHack, and NetHack — optimizing memory alone, without touching the agent's task-action behavior at all, improved the base agent roughly 2x to 4x, enough to bring a 32B open-weight model into competitive range with frontier systems like Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking. That's a strong demonstration that memory management is an independently learnable skill and a high-leverage target for anyone building long-horizon agents.

related.title: Language Models Need Sleep
related.hook: Humans consolidate the day's memories while sleeping. This paper gives LLMs a 'sleep' phase to distill fragile short-term context into stable long-term weights — and a 'dreaming' phase to rehearse.

related.title: MemSyco-Bench: Benchmarking Sycophancy in Agent Memory
related.hook: Agent memory sounds purely good — until retrieved memories start pushing an agent to agree with the user over the facts. MemSyco-Bench is built specifically to catch that failure.

flashcards.back_html: The cognitive-science idea of knowing what to encode, when to retrieve, and how to organize knowledge — applied to LLM agents by treating memory management as a trainable skill, not a fixed mechanism.
